Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn these field notes into an internal transit accessibility audit memo for the service planning and station operations teams? the audit is about the transfer path between Harbor Street bus interchange and the east entrance of Alder Quay rail station, visited on 14 May. keep it focused on the observed route and the access issues in these notes, not a general review of the whole station or bus network. please address it to Leonie, not Ellis. I need a usable draft that distinguishes what the team saw from what still needs checking, and doesn't make the missing measurements sound like confirmed findings.

context from the visit: two people walked the connection shortly after 8:00 in the morning, then one of them repeated the approach from the bus side at about 10:40. It was dry on both walks. The bus interchange has bays A through F along the north curb, with the rail entrance across Dock Lane, on the south side. We followed the signed pedestrian route rather than crossing wherever seemed shortest. Nobody timed the trip with a stopwatch, so don't give a precise journey time. One notebook calls the first walk “the busy one”; that was the note-taker's description, not a passenger count or a claim about a typical peak.

notes from the bus side: at bay C, the route marker fixed to the shelter post pointed toward the signal crossing, but the small map below it had a faded panel and the east entrance label was difficult to read from standing height. At bay D the same style of map was clearer, though partly hidden when two people were waiting by the post. There was no tactile ground surface indicator strip that we could identify between the waiting area and the curb ramp at C. We did not check under every shelter or establish whether a strip had been removed, so say only what was observed. A driver at a parked bus said, “people usually ask me which side the station is on.” We didn't record the driver's name or ask how often that happens.

crossing observations: the signed route leads from the north curb to a signal crossing on Dock Lane, then along the east pavement toward the station entrance. During the first walk a delivery van was stopped close to the curb ramp, narrowing the usable approach; it had left before the later repeat walk. The crossing button was on a pole to the right of the ramp. One auditor could reach it while standing, but we didn't test reach ranges or the signal timing. The audible signal could be heard during the first crossing, though traffic noise made it hard to distinguish near the center of the road. We did not establish whether the sound level changes across cycles. Don't turn that one observation into a claim that the signal is always audible or inaudible.

between the crossing and the entrance, the east pavement had a row of three temporary utility plates. The middle plate sat slightly proud of the surrounding surface, and the first auditor slowed down before stepping over it. We did not measure the height or check whether a mobility aid could pass over it. The pavement narrowed near the cycle rack; at the narrow point one person with a backpack could get through without turning sideways, but we didn't try a wheelchair or measure the clear width. A sandwich board for a cafe stood beyond the rack on the later walk, not the first. Keep the timing straight rather than implying the board was there throughout the visit.

entrance notes: the east entrance has two doors next to one another. The left-hand door was held open during the first walk, while the right-hand door was closed; on the later pass both were closed. We didn't test the opening force, door controls, or whether either door was locked. A sign inside the vestibule says the lift is on the left, but we didn't enter the station or verify the lift's location or operation. From outside, the sign was visible after approaching the doors but not from the crossing. Please distinguish that sign's wording from anything we confirmed about the lift.

one of the auditors wrote in the margin that the route “works if you already know where to look.” Keep that as an attributed impression, not a finding that all passengers have the same experience. The pair agreed that the faded map at C and the changing obstacles along the pavement deserve follow-up, but they did not rank them against each other or agree on a remedy. There were no interviews with passengers, no access tests using a mobility device, and no measurements of pavement width, plate height, door force, or signal timing. Mention those limits where relevant rather than turning them into a separate list of invented results.

could you organize the memo with a brief purpose and scope at the start, then a numbered section for the route observations, and a short section on items for follow-up? Keep the notes tied to their locations and times, and use ordinary language that station staff can act on. Include both quoted remarks exactly as recorded and attribute who said or wrote them where the notes identify that. The driver is unnamed, and the margin note is from one auditor, not a named person. Don't assign either quote to a particular auditor by name. Don't claim the auditors reached a conclusion about compliance, overall accessibility, or what should be installed.

for the follow-up part, carry forward the unresolved checks in the notes: whether tactile indicators are present elsewhere under the shelters or were removed, the visibility of the C map in ordinary use, the crossing button and audible signal under different conditions, the plates and clear pavement width, and the entrance doors and lift. The delivery van and cafe board are observations from different moments, so retain that distinction. The repeat approach was at about 10:40 and only from the bus side; don't describe it as a full second audit. If the memo states a fact, it should come from the notes above. I haven't supplied a site plan, standards checklist, passenger count, measurements, or a station response, so don't add those. End with the remaining checks, rather than a recommendation or a summary claiming the route is accessible or inaccessible.", "output": "Prepare an internal transit accessibility audit memo for the service planning and station operations teams, addressed to **Leonie, not Ellis**. The memo should cover the observed transfer route between Harbor Street bus interchange and the east entrance of Alder Quay rail station, visited on 14 May. Keep the scope to that route and the access issues in the supplied notes; do not turn it into a general review of the station or bus network. Distinguish direct observations from unresolved questions, and do not present missing measurements as confirmed findings.

Begin with a brief statement of purpose and scope. Then use a numbered section for route observations, followed by a short section on items for follow-up. Keep observations connected to their locations and times, use ordinary language for station staff, and include the quoted remarks exactly as recorded. Attribute each quote only as far as the notes allow: the driver is unnamed, and the margin note was written by one auditor, whose name is not supplied. End with the remaining checks, not a recommendation or a summary claiming that the route is accessible or inaccessible.

**Source notes**

Two people walked the connection shortly after 8:00 in the morning; one repeated the approach from the bus side at about 10:40. It was dry on both walks. Bus bays A through F run along the north curb of the interchange, and the rail entrance is across Dock Lane on the south side. The auditors followed the signed pedestrian route. They did not time the trip with a stopwatch, so do not state a precise journey time. One notebook describes the first walk as “the busy one”; this is the note-taker’s description, not a passenger count or a claim about a typical peak.

1. **Bus-side route and signs.** At bay C, the route marker fixed to the shelter post pointed toward the signal crossing. The small map below it had a faded panel, and the east entrance label was difficult to read from standing height. At bay D, the same style of map was clearer, though partly hidden when two people were waiting by the post. The auditors could not identify a tactile ground surface indicator strip between the waiting area and the curb ramp at C. They did not check under every shelter or establish whether a strip had been removed; describe only what they observed. A driver at a parked bus said, “people usually ask me which side the station is on.” The driver’s name was not recorded, and the auditors did not ask how often this happens.

2. **Dock Lane crossing.** The signed route goes from the north curb to a signal crossing on Dock Lane, then along the east pavement toward the station entrance. On the first walk, a delivery van was stopped close to the curb ramp, narrowing the usable approach. It had left before the later repeat walk. The crossing button was on a pole to the right of the ramp. One auditor could reach it while standing, but the auditors did not test reach ranges or signal timing. They could hear the audible signal during the first crossing, although traffic noise made it hard to distinguish near the center of the road. They did not establish whether its sound level changes across cycles. Do not generalize this observation into a claim that the signal is always audible or inaudible.

3. **East pavement and entrance.** Between the crossing and entrance, a row of three temporary utility plates was on the east pavement. The middle plate sat slightly proud of the surrounding surface, and the first auditor slowed before stepping over it. The auditors did not measure its height or check whether a mobility aid could pass over it. Near the cycle rack, the pavement narrowed. One person wearing a backpack could pass the narrow point without turning sideways, but the auditors did not try a wheelchair or measure clear width. A cafe sandwich board stood beyond the rack on the later walk, not the first; keep this timing distinct.

The east entrance has two adjacent doors. The left-hand door was held open during the first walk, while the right-hand door was closed. On the later pass, both doors were closed. The auditors did not test opening force, door controls, or whether either door was locked. A sign inside the vestibule says the lift is on the left. The auditors did not enter the station or verify the lift’s location or operation. The sign was visible from outside after approaching the doors, but not from the crossing. Distinguish the wording on the sign from anything confirmed about the lift.

One auditor wrote in the margin, “works if you already know where to look.” Present this as an attributed impression, not as a finding about all passengers’ experiences. The pair agreed that the faded map at C and the changing pavement obstacles deserve follow-up, but did not rank them or agree on a remedy. There were no passenger interviews, tests using a mobility device, or measurements of pavement width, plate height, door force, or signal timing. Mention relevant limitations without turning them into invented results.

In the follow-up section, carry forward the unresolved checks: whether tactile indicators are present elsewhere under the shelters or were removed; the C map’s visibility in ordinary use; the crossing button and audible signal under different conditions; the plates and clear pavement width; and the entrance doors and lift. Preserve the difference between the delivery van and cafe board observations: they were present at different times. The repeat approach was at about 10:40 and only from the bus side, not a full second audit. Use no facts beyond these notes. No site plan, standards checklist, passenger count, measurements, or station response was supplied."}]
